eligibility_reason: MAGE stores the agent's own action-observation trace and derived subgoal summaries in a persistent tree at run time (Grow, Compress; Section 3, p. 4) and later reconstructs its execution state by reading the active root-to-current path on subsequent steps to condition future actions (p. 2, p. 4). This is an LLM-based agent (ReAct with a Qwen backbone, p. 7) that writes and reads its own externalised store across steps, published 2026, in English, with retrievable full text — satisfies I1-I4. Not E2/E3: the store is agent-written, not a fixed corpus (contrasted explicitly with static RAG corpora, p. 3). Not E4/E5/E6/E7: a novel 17-page method paper with memory as the stated contribution, evaluated empirically (p. 7).

facets.justification: MAGE writes a two-layer hierarchical execution-state tree: a bottom layer of raw action-observation nodes and a top layer of subgoal summary nodes, built by explicit parent/child node operations (Section 3.1-3.2, p. 4; Algorithm 1, p. 7). The paper explicitly distinguishes this from graph-based agent memory that organizes entries 'through entity or event relations' (Section 2.2, p. 3) and from vector stores retrieved by embedding similarity (p. 1, p. 3) — it is a state-management tree, not a semantic/knowledge graph, so none of the listed store types fit cleanly.

Compress 'moves completed raw segments from R into top-layer summaries in C, freeing context while preserving subgoal boundaries' (Section 3.2, p. 4), which is the mechanism the paper credits with bounding context growth (Abstract, p. 1; p. 4). Grow (append) and Revise (delete/restore to a boundary, an edit-in-place operation, Algorithm 1 R EVISE, p. 7) also transform the store, but the paper's headline claim and token-reduction result (55.1%, p. 1, p. 7) are attributed to the grow+compress boundary-aware compression cycle.

The execution state is read by traversing the tree from root to the current node — an exact structural traversal, not a ranking: 'the current execution state is read from the active tree path instead of being assembled from semantically similar entries' (Section 1, p. 2); Algorithm 1's TRACE and FLATTEN operations walk cover_nodes/parent pointers along this path (p. 7).

MAGE is evaluated on the MemoryArena benchmark against six baseline systems (HippoRAG2, MemoRAG, Mem0, ReasoningBank, MemoryOS, SimpleMem) with a fixed backbone LLM and controlled hyperparameters, reporting success rate, progress score and token consumption (Section 4, p. 7). No deployment, real users, or fielded setting is reported in the given pages — this is a lab benchmark comparison.

Section 4 (p. 7) runs a fixed task suite (MemoryArena, four domains) across MAGE and multiple baselines under identical model/hardware settings and reports scored metrics (SR, PS, token count) in a results table, matching benchmark evaluation rather than a single manipulated-condition experiment.

The contribution list (Section 1, p. 2) names the technique itself: 'We propose MAGE, which organizes agentic memory as a two-layer hierarchical tree... We design four coupled operations that make this tree an agent-manipulable object.' The contribution argued for is the mechanism, not a released tool or a dataset (MemoryArena is cited as an existing benchmark, not this paper's contribution).
